Eggs of Auckland teal maintained at 39 °C [T = 39 °C] hatch after a developmental period of 28 days [ab = 28 days], an incubation duration that is somewhat prolonged compared to other small Anatidae, likely reflecting the cool and variable thermal conditions of the subantarctic islands they inhabit. The newly emerged ducklings weigh approximately 62 grams [Ww0 = approximately 62 grams] at hatching, a modest neonatal mass for an island dabbling duck, reflecting the energetic constraints of egg production in a resource-limited subantarctic environment. Once hatched, the altricial nestlings are brooded intensively by the female, and within the first few weeks they undergo a rapid phase of mass gain, gradually developing the downy plumage essential for thermoregulation. The timing of hatching is often synchronized with local invertebrate abundance, maximizing food availability for the rapidly growing brood. Field studies indicate that the parental birds engage in frequent feeding trips, primarily foraging on coastal invertebrates and small crustaceans to meet the energetic demands of their offspring. The initial weight of the duckling is a critical determinant of early survival, as heavier hatchlings exhibit superior thermoregulatory capacity and greater competitive success during feeding interactions.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the ducklings reach the key developmental milestone of fledging at 53 days after hatching [tx = 53 days after hatching], with some individuals recorded as early as 50 days and others taking up to 55 days to achieve sustained flight. This relatively extended nestling period is characteristic of a species that invests heavily in offspring quality over quantity, and it allows for the full development of flight feathers and foraging skills before independence. Following fledging, the young birds enter a critical juvenile phase during which they refine their hunting techniques and gradually disperse from the natal territory. The precise timing of fledging is influenced by local food resources and weather conditions, as the ducklings require a steady supply of high-protein prey to complete feather development. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the fledging period of Auckland teal is among the longest for dabbling ducks of comparable body size, reflecting the challenges of life in a resource-limited island environment. Parental care continues for several weeks post-fledging, with adults occasionally provisioning the young as they learn to forage independently.

Sexual maturation in Auckland teal is a gradual process, with puberty attained at approximately 159 days after hatching [tp = approximately 159 days after hatching] when the birds are maintained at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively late onset of reproductive maturity, compared to many other members of the genus Anas, is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth and the accumulation of sufficient body reserves before committing to the high energetic costs of reproduction. The female ducks reach an ultimate adult weight of 410 grams [Wwi = 410 grams], while the males achieve a slightly larger maximal adult body mass of 521 grams [Wwi = 521 grams]. This modest sexual size dimorphism, with males being roughly 27% heavier than females, is typical of monogamous waterfowl species where male–male competition for territories is present but not extreme. The larger body size of males may confer advantages in defending nesting sites and securing access to high-quality foraging areas during the breeding season. Both sexes undergo a complete pre-basic molt after the breeding season, during which they are flightless for several weeks, a vulnerable period that restricts them to well-protected wetland refuges.

First reproduction in Auckland teal occurs after a substantial period of juvenile development, with the initial brood produced at 511 days after hatching [tR = 511 days after hatching], when the birds are maintained at a core temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delayed onset of breeding allows the young birds to achieve full adult body mass and establish a stable territory in the densely vegetated coastal habitats they prefer. The reproductive output of this species is relatively modest, with females laying 5 to 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 5 to 6 eggs per clutch] and producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year], a strategy that reflects the constraints of a short breeding season in a cool, unpredictable climate. This annual reproductive rate is consistent with a K-selected life-history strategy, where parental investment per offspring is high and adult survival is prioritized over maximizing yearly fecundity. The eggs are laid in a well-concealed nest among dense tussock grass or sedges, and the female alone undertakes the incubation duties, leaving the nest only briefly to feed during the 28-day incubation period. The success of each clutch is highly dependent on the local predator community, with introduced mammalian predators being a major source of nest failure.

The resting metabolic rate of Auckland teal, measured as basal oxygen consumption, has been recorded at 337.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 337.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that aligns with the generally reduced metabolic intensity observed in island-endemic waterfowl compared to their continental counterparts. This relatively low metabolic rate is likely an adaptation to the limited and seasonally variable food resources of the subantarctic islands, allowing the birds to minimize daily energetic requirements during periods of scarcity. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is 18.6 years [am = 18.6 years], a remarkable longevity for a dabbling duck of moderate body size, which underscores a life-history strategy built around high adult survival, delayed reproduction, and low annual fecundity at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The oldest individuals are typically those that hold prime breeding territories in the most productive coastal wetlands, where they have consistent access to prey. This combination of a modest metabolic rate and an extended lifespan is characteristic of species that have evolved under conditions of low extrinsic mortality, where the probability of surviving from one year to the next is relatively high. Field studies on the Auckland Islands have documented individual birds returning to the same nesting sites for over a decade.
